utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam and good morning to you, too. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can indeed following the proceeding in my own mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and also good morning to the learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, we represent Mr. Oric. We are here together with our legal assistant, Mrs. Adisa Mehic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you and your team. As you would have certainly noticed already, we are missing Judge Eser as well today, again today. The reason is that the personal family problem that he is encountering at the moment encountered some slight complications over the weekend, and after consultation with me and of course with Judge Brydensholt as well, yesterday I told him to stay at home, and we will see how the situation unfolds on a daily basis. There is a likelihood that he will turn up in the course of this week but I have strongly advised him against it, which would put us in the position where we would have to sit without him for the rest of this week, Friday excluded because we are not going to sit on Friday if we manage to finish with the two. We also agreed that he will be following the proceedings from home and the agreement is to make sure that your client is not in any way prejudiced that, if at any time he would wish to have this witness and the next one recalled for some questions by him, we will do that. Alternatively, if you would like us to put some questions to the two witnesses on his behalf, we will do that. I'm not saying that he will not turn up this week but if he asks for my advice I'm going to advise him to stay where he is and tend to his problem. I hope you understand and that you are cooperative in this. I can assure you it's not something that we like but it's something that we can hardly avoid. He also insists that we go ahead without him if I insist that he stays at home. All right? That is the position. So we will be sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis with which you are familiar, and we will continue to sit until he returns but, of course, not beyond the statutory or the period established by the rules. So that's the position. Any comments on your part?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. We do understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you it's not a slight problem. Otherwise we would have dealt with it in a different manner. Mr. Wubben you don't have a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, that having been said, that being said, are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a minor issue. I was advised by my doctors today, or rather during the summer, that if I sit for a long time, I might have a crisis and if we need to cross-examine the witnesses for a long time I would like to be able to be allowed to sit. Actually, correction: If I stand for a long time I would have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have already told you before that that is not a problem. Don't even need to remind us, Madam Vidovic. Please make yourself comfortable because there is no sense trying to be formalistic when it hurts. So. Any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's bring the witness in, and we keep our fingers crossed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, good morning to you. Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may have noticed that I'm speaking in the English language and what I'm saying is being simultaneously translated into French and into your own language. I want to make sure first and foremost that you are receiving the translation, the interpretation, in your language or in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that it is loud and clear enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time the reception is impaired, if it's not reaching you or if the sound level is too low or too high, please draw our attention straight away and we will rectify the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome once more. You are about to start giving evidence as one of the witnesses summoned by the accused, Naser Oric, in this case. And our Rules require that before you start your evidence, you enter a solemn declaration, in the sense that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath in several domestic jurisdictions. Madam Usher, who is standing to your right, will be giving you the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down, make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll try to explain to you what's going to happen. First of all let me introduce myself I'm the Presiding Judge, my name is Carmel Agius and I come from the Mediterranean island of Malta. To my right I have Judge Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark. Usually to my left I have Judge Professor Albin Eser from German but he couldn't be with us today because of urgent personal matters and therefore we are going to sit with two judges only. To your right there is the Prosecution team and to your left there is the Defence team. Since you have been summoned by the Defence, you are first going to be examined by being required to answer a number of questions by a member of the Defence team. Who is it going to be? Madam Vidovic, who I suppose you have already met. When her examination-in-chief is finished, then you will be cross-examined by Mr. Jan Wubben who is the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case. Your duty in terms of our Rules and also -- and particularly so -- in terms and pursuant to your solemn declaration is to answer all questions truthfully and to the best of your ability irrespective of who is putting the question to you. In other words, you do not have a right to draw a distinction between questions that are being put to you by the Defence and questions which are being put to you by the Prosecution. You are to treat them the same and provide us with a truthful and a comprehensive answer. My last advice to you before we start is, if you want to go home according to schedule, please try to answer the questions that are put to you, the whole question and nothing but the question. Don't try to give us more information than you are asked in any particular question because that would mean you staying here for days and days and days. Madam Vidovic will go first.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I move on to the cross-examination [as interpreted], since we both speak the same language, let me point out to you that it is necessary for you to allow for a slight break between my question and your answer in order to make sure that the interpreters have enough time to interpret both the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the course of these questions, I am going to lead the witness when it comes to his personal data, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you were born in the village of Poznanovici on the 7th of April 1961, actually in a hamlet called Podkorjen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your father is Adem and your mother is Dila?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your mother's maiden name is Malkic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You finished primary school at Fakovici in 1976?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thereupon you finished grammar school at Srebrenica in 1981?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did your military service on the island of Lastovo in the then Socialist Republic of Croatia in the infantry in 1981; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from the faculty of philosophy at Tuzla Technical and Information Department and you graduated in 1999 -- 1989?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After finishing grammar school, you worked at the factory of Akumulator at Potocari as a technical controller where you stayed until 1983, or rather between 1983 and August 1985?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, you pursued your studies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you left your job at the said factory in 1985, you opened your own shop in the place called Podkorijen-Poznanovici, which you kept until the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Today, you work in the sector of education. You teach at information technology at the first primary school of Zivinice?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You spent the war years at Podkorjen and Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica, you, together with a group of other people, were taken prisoner on the 22nd of July 1995 and you went -- you have been to two Serb camps, more specifically Karakaj, Zvornik, and Batkovic, near Bijeljina, and that's where you had a very hard time and you did not even want to discuss that period of time with me. You didn't want to remember it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica, in 1995, your father was taken prisoner and he was killed at Kozluk. Your uncle and his sons were also killed as well as your mother's brothers and as well as many other male relatives, including three of your wife's brothers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I am going to show you a map of the area of Srebrenica now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please circulate the map. And if we could have a copy of the map shown to the witness, and it is now going to be easier for us to follow his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you've got the map on the ELMO? It's to your left. Could you turn to your left, please? Mr. Ramic, I would like to ask you first of all to show me your own village, Poznanovici, or rather in your hamlet Podkorjen on the map, and can you put a circle around it on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be given a pen?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Podkorjen. Thank you very much. I would like to ask you now to tell the Trial Chamber what villages are situated in this part of the area east of Srebrenica in relative proximity of your village. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Next to my village, Podkorjen, or rather this is a part of the Poznici [phoen] area, but there are two other villages there, Dedici and Karici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Ramic, show us where approximately would Dedici and Karici be since we are talking about tiny villages that are not marked on the map? But could you perhaps mark the approximate position by an X here?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, this is Poznanovici and between Poznanovic and here there is Dedici and then Donji Karici, lower Karici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the witness has encircled the two villages of Podkorjen and Poznanovici, and, in between, he has marked on the map, which is being given Defence Exhibit number D7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 721, two crosses. The one at the left, that is the one nearest -- nearer to the village of Podkorjen is the village of Dedici, and the other X or cross is the village of Karici. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now, sir, to show to the Trial Chamber the other Muslim villages, such as Osmace, if that indeed is a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have Osmace and Derovskis [phoen], Stozersko, et cetera. I'm going to show you Osmace now. This is Osmace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the witness encircles the village of Osmace on the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us the village of Skenderovici, sir?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Skenderovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the record the witness encircles the village of Skenderovici on the map, D721.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Muslim villages belonging to the area of Skenderovici are Dimnici, Stozersko, and Subin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, and for the record, the witness also encircles the villages of Dimnici, Stozersko, and Subin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show the Trial Chamber the village of Mocevici, and could you tell us if that too is a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mocevici that's also a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what about Brezovica, is it a Muslim village too?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Brezovica is over here. Just let me find it. Kulici as well. That is a village that was a part of the Brezovica area, and then Lokve.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you see Brezovica itself?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Here we have Brezovica. This was the name of the entire area, so it's in italics.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness encircles on the map the area denoted as Brezovica and the villages of Lokva and Kulici. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I would like to ask you now to show us the villages that used to be inhabited by the Serb population before the war in that area.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that the Serb villages were Ratkovici, Dvorista, Ducici, Polinci, Kaludra, Grujcici, Stanatovici, Tanesavici [phoen], Magdovici, Oparci, Spat, Pribicevac, Brezani, Turija.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you underline the names of those villages for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can you give him a different colour, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... distinguishes itself. Yes. Mr. Ramic, as you mark or encircle these places, could you please repeat the name of each village and one after the other? All right? Thank you. Go ahead. You mark on the map the villages that were predominantly inhabited by Serbian or ... Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the village of Ratkovici here. Dvorista, Ducici, Polinci, Magdovici, Oparci, Vranesevici, Kaludra, Obarak, Grujcici, then to the east we have Seona, Popovici, Mlecva, and Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Stanatovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Stanatovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Spat earlier?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we will see Spat. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Below you have Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Pribicevac, yes, we have Turija, Brezani. These are villages that are close to the Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, at the top of the map, in this white area, could you please write down your initials? Thank you. And can you keep the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will be needing the map later so can the map stay in front of the witness? We will go back to the map later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, I'm going to ask you now, can you explain to the Trial Chamber how far is it from Poznanovici to Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The distance is about three and a half kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if you go along the road, it's about three and a half kilometres?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: If you go along the road but as the crow flies it's very close.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please now explain to the Trial Chamber the configuration of the terrain on one side from Ratkovici, Ducici and Palimac [phoen], and on the other side, Dedici, Poznanovici, and Karovici [phoen], whereby you can use the map if you think that that will assist you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: On the map here, there is this white area between Poznanovici and Ratkovici which indicates that these are elevations. From these elevations, we could see Serb villages of Ratkovici on one side and then on the other side we can see Poznanovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If someone were to claim that the Muslim villages in that area, and I'm thinking of Poznanovici, Dedici, and Podkorjen, were at an elevation in relation to the Serb villages that are in the valley, would that be true?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, what is the position of the villages?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The position of the Serb villages, Ratkovici and Poznanovici, actually they are at one altitude. When you climb up to an elevation, you can both see Serb and Muslim villages. So no villages are higher than some other villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, if I understood you properly, what you are saying is that they are more or less at the same altitude above sea level?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we will go back to this detail when we use the map again. But now I want to ask you something else. Mr. Ramic, before the conflict broke out in the spring of 1992, was this a quiet, peaceful area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long before the war did you have your shop that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were selling the items in your shop, did you have contacts with a lot of people?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The citizens of all the Serb villages would come to my shop, including Ratkovici and Poznanovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the war broke out in 1992, were there any nationalist excesses amongst the Muslim population in this area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any such incidents amongst the Serb population in the period from 1990 onwards?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. With the arrival of Slobodan Milosevic, they carried the photograph of Slobodan Milosevic and glorified Serb-hood.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of 1990, have any knowledge about whether anybody was arming themselves in your area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the Serb and Muslim population came to my shop, there was a lot of talk or there was often talk that Serbs were arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs conceal the fact that they were arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but there were some situations where information came out that they were arming themselves. There was even a silly situation when a Serb came to my shop and asked me, "Are you issuing weapons?" And I said, "Well, who is issuing weapons?" And he said, "The army," probably thinking of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you found out that Serbs in the Ratkovici area were arming themselves, was that something that worried you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did worry us. However, I and many other inhabitants in the area thought that there would be no war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, did you hear about any incidents in the area of Bratunac and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In September 1991, on the Bratunac-Kravica road at the Kajici settlement, two Muslims were killed in an ambush as they were driving along in their car. That day, I had the opportunity to find that out because I was travelling on the same road to Tuzla so the police informed me what happened and that I couldn't actually pass along that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the Muslim population frightened by this incident?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslim population was concerned, and they thought that something terrible was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that event, did you use this road through Kravica at all?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, because we were afraid. The road to Tuzla via Kravica was avoided by the Muslim population. They used detours. They used macadam roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, did this incident increase the tensions in that whole Podrinje region?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The tensions were higher in that whole region, in that period, yes. People were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the conduct of the media in late 1991 and early 1992 until the war broke out, based on what you could hear?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: In my area of Poznanovici there was information making the rounds. We were covered by Television Belgrade signals. It was not so easy to hear or see Sarajevo programmes. So there was a lot of information from Belgrade that in that area, in Poznanovic and Osmace, there were a lot of Green Berets, that there was a concentration of Green Berets, and that in that area there were even some 5.000 Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was actually the truth?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The truth was that in our Poznanovici, we only had five or six hunting rifles, some pistols.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any kind of military formation present there? Were there any Green Berets there?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. There were no military formations at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how did the Serb population react to this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: They kept asking us were there any Green Berets and where were they. And we kept telling them that there was no military formation at all in our area. There could be no talk of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, from the village of Poznanovici, including your Podkorjen, did you tell anything to the Serbs about this concern of theirs about the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We proposed to hold joint village guards to convince them that there were no military formations at all in our villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you agree to set up these joint guards?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We agreed to set up joint guards. I mentioned that place on the map, it was a place called Stub A.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show the Trial Chamber again where Stub A is? This area, is this an area that you are calling Stub A, is there such an area, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's an elevation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show the Trial Chamber, if you can, where this elevation is?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I'm going to circle that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, Madam Vidovic. For the record, the witness marks a dark circle, small, dark circle in green, above the circle around the village of Poznanovici, and indicates this as the area known as Stub A. Yes. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, could you please tell us what you could see from Stub A, if you could see anything at all?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, you could see the Serb villages of Ratkovici and Poznanovici, and also the access road from Osmace from that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How much time did these joint guard duties continue?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: For two nights, two days, two nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber why this went on for only two days and two nights?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The conclusion that I reached, and others who were on guard duty with me, was that they only came for two nights to the joint guard duty in order to see what kind of weapons we had available.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to this joint guard duty, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had automatic weapons, and of the three of them, one of them even had a machine-gun, while we only had hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Except for these three men, did you notice any other men nearby?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the background, actually behind us, not too far from us, I noticed that there were many other armed and uniformed Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were they behind you or behind these three Serbs who had come to be on guard duty with you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: They were completely behind us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people who came for the guard duty, the Serbs, did they have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had olive drab uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, did you know any of these people who came for guard duty that night? I'm thinking of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Blagoje Prodanovic from Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your assessment, what kind of a neighbour was he?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Compared to the others, I could see that he was trying to maintain good relations between us, that he was better than the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him and, if you did, when did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: We talked on the second night, during the guard duty. That was when we talked. We discussed weapons and he told us that they were issued weapons at the Ruljevici elementary school, Ruljevici or Vranesevici, that they had had training down there and that he did not want to wage war against the Muslims. I had the impression that he was intoxicated and that at one point he even gave us his automatic rifle because when he saw that we only had hunting weapons, he gave it to us so that we could defend ourselves. He didn't want to wage war against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, can you remember when was this, which month was this, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: This was April.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that he told you here is a rifle so that you can defend yourselves, did any of the other Serbs react to that? Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since they heard that Blagoje said that somebody from the background, one of those Serb soldiers that I was talking about, uncocked their rifle and said that the guards should disband, that they would be going to Ratkovici -- we would be going to Ratkovici, they would be going to Poznanovici, and that there would be no more guard duty so that Blagoje also had to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Milenko Zivanovic before the war and his family?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew General Milenko Zivanovic and his family well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Milenko Zivanovic was born in Ratkovici, the hamlet of Ratkovici, which is part of the village of Ducici. Here on the map you can see where Ducici is. That's where he grew up. He was our next-door neighbour in Podkorjen. The distance between Podkorjen and Ducici is about three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the war, did Milenko Zivanovic keep company with any of the Muslims from Podkorjen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a best man Adem Osmanovic in Podkorjen, and he would see him often and he also would visit Mehmed Osmanovic, Efendija.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he was an officers of the JNA before the war?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that he was a senior officer in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he come to the Ratkovici area and the Poznanovici area at some time, maybe a few months before the war?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came several times in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see him in that period and, if you did, when was that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: It was in 1991, late 1991, it was winter. I remember he talked to me in the shop. My shop was actually in my house. So we had this conversation. I and General Milenko Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. And what did he tell you, then?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: General Zivanovic told me then, "Look, see what the nationalist parties did. They've caused quarrels amongst the people. They've created this war. The army will not allow them to make war." I guess that he was thinks about the officers of the JNA, and I confirmed that. I said that this is something that should not happen and that these Serb and Muslim villages were always on good terms, in good relations, and that there should be no escalation of the conflict in this area. It shouldn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that conversation in your shop, did you notice anything characteristic about his conduct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: When he came into the shop and he was looking at all the items, he kept looking at the counters in the shop and he was trying to see if he would see any weapons anywhere. I understood that he was looking for weapons because in that area there was a lot of talk about weapons. Unfortunately, I didn't have anything else other than the legal pistol that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if anything happened in the course of February, March, and April, 1992, in Ducici and Ratkovici, if anything did happen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Several times, helicopters landed in the Serbian villages of Ratkovici and Ducici, and I actually saw one of these helicopters landing into the village of Ducici. I watched it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out why these helicopters were landing?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: My neighbour, Mehmed Mehanovic, told me that at that time he was not too far from that helicopter in the woods. He was doing something. And then he saw that weapons were being unloaded from the helicopter, machine-guns, mortars, rifles, and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, could you tell us whether these helicopters had any particular markings on them that would make them distinguishable from other helicopters of the same make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's interesting, and I can say that today, because I saw that. They did have markings but those helicopters that did have the markings, that seemed to be just a cover.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The question of the Judges was what kind of markings did they have?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had markings by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you talk to any of the Serbs about this?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked with Blagoje Prodanovic. I mentioned earlier that he said that they were arming themselves, that they were getting weapons at the Huljevic [phoen] or Njesevic [phoen] elementary school and that that was where they were going to for training.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court Usher now show the witness Defence Exhibit D690? Pages 175 to 177. This is a book by Mr. Ibisevic, and these are pages 24 and 25 in English of the chapter 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what -- I'm sorry to interrupt you again, Madam Vidovic, but this is what I meant last time by trying to suggest to you to try and eliminate as much as possible cross-references because this document now it seems we have it twice. One is a Prosecution exhibit, which we received last week from Mr. Wubben or from the Prosecution anyway and which we gave a new exhibit number, and one is from the Defence, which is already marked as D690. I am not in a position, because I'm not an expert in this, to ensure that the two translations are identical. So I am just alerting you to this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what we agreed, Mr. Wubben and I, is that I will check the translation that they provided, and it's not a problem to use -- for us to use the P exhibit, but we do need a little bit of time. And I apologise but I really have to use this document today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed with 690 for the time being. If either of you detect any differences in the relevant parts, in the translation of the relevant parts, please draw our attention. We'll try and do the same exercise ourselves as well. But it's important for you to keep this in mind. All right? Let's proceed. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, could you please look at page 175 and 176? I'm going to read out two small parts to you. "Semso Jusic, member of the municipal assembly of the village of Poznanovici told me that there had been shooting above his village the night before. The Bosniaks of Poznanovici spent the night in the open guarding their village. He also informed me that the Serbs from Fakovici had a store of weapons and ammunition stashed in an abandoned schoolhouse near the village of Ruljevici, the municipality of Bratunac. The Serbs had received the arms from the JNA. Some Bosniaks had seen military lorries arriving in a village earlier. I promised Semso that I would personally go to Ruljevici and check whether these claims about the weapons were true because the Bosnians knew the truth." I would just like to draw your attention that this event was noted down in Mr. Ibisevic's diary as Friday, the 3rd of April 1992. Another part in the Bosnian version I'm going to read, the author states, "I am Besim Ibisevic, chairman of the municipal assembly of the -- of Srebrenica, and I was sent here by the National Defence Council to check what is being kept in this building. We want to know whether there are any weapons there and paramilitary units and we have to report about this to the people in our municipality. Every night there is shooting from here in the direction of Poznanovici and people are disturbed. One of the guards replied that there were no paramilitaries there and that they were only guarding weapons in the school house. To my question where they could -- whether we could personally look at the weapons, we were told that we could not. We have told you ourselves that there are weapons here, but it doesn't matter how much." Mr. Ramic, my question to you is as follows: Do you know Mr. Semso Jusic from the village of Poznanovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is my cousin and he was a deputy in the municipal assembly of Srebrenica in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that period, that is to say the beginning of April 1992, do you remember whether at that time you Muslims from the area of Poznanovic talked to Mr. Jusic about the arming of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, We did, and we suggested he informs the municipality of the municipal assembly of Srebrenica about those events as a matter of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did these events, this shooting, have to do with some villagers from your area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, our village of Poznanovici, the inhabitants had had to leave their houses on a number of occasions and they had to spend the night in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is the shooting with regard to the Serb villages that it was coming from?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: It used to come from the village of Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Ms. -- the first -- for the record, because you mentioned page 17 something or whatever, but for the record in our English version of the D690, the first excerpt that you read out to the witness is contained in the entry for Friday, the 3rd of April 1992, on page 24 of the English text. The second one, I haven't managed to find as yet. If you could give me -- is it the same date or is it a different date?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the second excerpt is on page 25 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second aspect -- second excerpt is in the -- roughly in the middle of the second paragraph on page 25 of the English text, that is Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit D690. Yes. In the middle of the paragraph starting with, "I am Besim Ibisevic, chairman of the municipal assembly." Yes, thank you. Do you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think we are okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break now, please, 25 minutes. --- Break taken at 10.05 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I would like to state on behalf of the Prosecution that Mr. Wubben has been advised to return home by a doctor. It appears that he has a viral infection and stands the possibility of being out of court for the next two or three days. I've informally informed the Defence of that situation but now I would like to just bring it to the attention of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information, Ms. Sellers. Only thing I want to know is the following - and, of course, you will find us cooperative as we always try to be - that at the beginning of the sitting I asked who was going to take over the witness for cross-examination and it was going to be Mr. Wubben. So I suppose you won't finish -- you will finish your examination-in-chief today, no? Madam Vidovic? Or you plan to at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am going to try and finish the examination-in-chief by all means today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So let's agree on this: That I would suppose your cross-examination was not intended to last more than a sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you think either of you or whoever, because of course I cannot decide for you, would be in a position to take over the witness for cross-examination tomorrow many?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will take over the cross-examination of the witness done by Mr. Wubben. There is a possibility, as I expressed to the Defence, that we might ask nor a slight delay of an hour, if necessary, to gather any other material, but we will try our best to stay within the time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you encounter difficulties then obviously you draw our attention to that and we will react in a rational way, I would imagine. I mean -- yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I asked of Mrs. Sellers was to take account of the fact that this witness has been here for a while. He's been in The Hague for 11 days already and he asked us to do all we could to make sure that he can return home as soon as possible because he has his other obligations to attend to and he also doesn't feel all that comfortable here. He has difficulty sleeping. So we would like to ask the Prosecution team to maybe take this into consideration and if they manage to do so we could have another witness here before Friday. So if they can possibly get organised in such a way as to finish tomorrow it would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was going to take on the part of the Prosecution the next witness, not this one, the next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson will be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. So that is not a problem either. All right, let's move, let's not waste or lose more time. If you are in a position to start tomorrow, then we go ahead. If you're not in a position we send the witness home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do intend to start tomorrow. I think that any rescheduling would be extremely minimum. We would try to accommodate both the witness and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. So Madam Vidovic, and I'm keeping my fingers crossed. I'll ask someone to come and bless the courtroom. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, we talked a short while ago about a part of this book by Mr. Ibisevic in this respect, and we stopped halfway as it were. So in relation to that I would like to put the following question to you: Is it correct that you noticed the arrival of military trucks to Ruljevici and that weapons were being unloaded from those trucks as it says in the book?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite true. In my conversation with Semso and some other people present we talked about those weapons and we knew that and people were talking about their arrival of those military trucks to Ruljevici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that what is stated in this part of the book, that is to say the fact that the locals in Poznanovici heard some shooting, I mean you've already confirmed that, but how do you know that those shots were being fired from Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew that because there were some boys who went to the hills above and there were following the situation on a daily basis. They were observing what was going on and they knew exactly that the shooting came from Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you about that in person?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramic, do you recollect any other event in the course of that period between the end of March and the beginning of April 1992 in your area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that shooting, which was something that we experienced on a daily basis, at a certain point I found out that not far away from us, in Fakovici, Mr. Kadrija who was a well-respected intellectual and Muslim went missing and he was taken in the direction of Zljebac and then all trace of him was lost and we still don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name Ognjen Markovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the son of Andrija Markovic from Fakovici. I knew him and his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Madam Vidovic slow down because I can sense that it's becoming difficult for the interpreters to catch up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, may I ask you once again to make sure that you allow for a short break after my question and then you answer. Now I'm going to ask you the following question: How do you remember Ognjen Markovic from that particular period of time? What do you remember about him?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, after that shooting that we complained about to the municipal assembly, Ognjen Markovic, called Bato, came to Poznanovici with another four Serb soldiers and they were armed, heavily armed, and they came to our village, and he went to see the teacher, Mr. Dzevad, and at that time he was asking around about whether any of the Muslims had taken any weapons, who was the leader of the SDS party, whether anyone was cutting down any trees from the woods, and he was acting like he owned the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss this with Mr. Dzevad Malkic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked about it with Dzevad Malkic straight away and he told me that Bato asked him to tell him about who had gotten weapons and then he answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As to Ognjen Markovic's behaviour, what about the elderly people? Did they give you any advice, the elders from your village, did they give you any advice about that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The elders did give us some advice because they knew exactly that it was just a provocation in order to provoke a conflict and they told us not to be provoked and not to give them any reason to engage in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you give them any such reason?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. Not -- none at the time, even though Markovic at that time went on to Ratkovici and then he came back through our village and went to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramic, do you remember what went on after Bosnia and Herzegovina was internationally recognised, what went on in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The situation worsened. It was a very difficult situation. We were faced with lots of refugees coming from those border areas. I mean, we already knew what was happening in the area of Bijeljina, Zvornik and Bratunac so it was quite clear to us what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where the first refugees start coming from?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The first refugees started coming from the area of Skelani, Dobraka [phoen], Klijesce, and the other villages around Skelani, the closest villages to us, along the River Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those were Muslims villages?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were Muslim villages, that's what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you about what happened to him in April and in the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told horrible tales about murder, rape, and the entire Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. families being torched alive in their houses or killed off altogether and I remember a woman called Zehra from Podkorjen, apparently she was killed together with her two sons who were just children.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell me about how many refugees arrived at your house, just to your house? Could you tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very many refugees arrived from the Skelani villages to our area, all along the river of Drina. And there were more than 30 refugees in my house alone, plus eight members of my own family.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how big was your house?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Seven by eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So 56 square metres.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic if someone were to claim that those Muslims from Skelani villages left their homes and their properties of their own volition, would you feel that it was true on the basis of the tales that you heard from them?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. That is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did many of these people stay outdoors in the woods and forests above the Skelani villages? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few of them stayed in the forests because I said earlier on that the houses were overcrowded and so there wasn't enough space and many hoped they would be able to return to their homes pretty soon so that's why they stayed in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And at that same period of time, May and June, 1992, did refugees from other areas start arriving to your village?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the municipality of Bratunac, Suha Hranca, Voljavica, Bjelovac, Biljaca, Tegari, Olica, Abdulici, Zanjevo, and all those other Muslim villages along Drina. So all those refugees were coming to our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you about what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told the same story as the refugees from the area of Skelani, that is to say the men being separated and sent to camps, murders, rapes, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If someone were to claim that those people from the villages along the River Drina also left their villages of their own free will, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask the usher to show the witness the document which refers to the command of the Brezani Brigade dated the 28th of May 1992, where we've got a signature by the commander Svetozar Andric. It is 04276215. It is an order issued by Svetozar Andric addressed to the TO headquarters of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, isn't it correct that I showed you this document before? Now I'd like to draw your attention to item 6 and 7 of this order and let me quote, "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and coordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out whilst men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange. The commanders of the aforementioned units are to be instructed regarding their specific tasks." And my question now, Mr. Ramic, my question to you in relation to this is the following: You told us that you talked to the refugees who had come to your area, quite a few of them. Did they tell you about the fact that their moving out was organised?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did indeed mention that. They said that first of all an ultimatum was given and they had to relinquish their arms. Once they had relinquished their arms, units would come into the villages and would separate men and women and children, and horrific acts were being perpetrated, rapes and so on, so it is indeed true that this was done in an organised way. People were chased away and they did it together with the SDS, the police, and the local population that was not involved with the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you heard that from the refugees?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that from the refugees. It was part of their stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could you just give a number to this document now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which consists of two pages, one in the original language, B/C/S, and the other one the corresponding translation in English, with ERN number respectively 04276215 and 6216 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D722. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, could you look at the map once again in case you still have it, the map you had earlier on? I'm going to ask you to indicate some of the villages specifically and I'm going to put the following question to you. You told us about the refugees from the Drina villages and in relation to that I'm going to put the following question to you. Is it correct that in the course of the months of April and May 1992, most of the Muslim villages in that area had been ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that the Muslim villages around Bratunac, Voljavica, Zalazje, Gornja Olica, Tegari, Bjelovac, Abdulici, Zanjevo, and I mentioned the villages of Skelani, they were ethnically cleansed. It's indeed true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you show the Trial Chamber on the map what was left of the Muslim villages in that area, in the month of June -- the end of May and the month of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Precisely the villages that I've marked in the beginning. Do I need to mark them again?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just going to ask you to tell us what happened to Mocevici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It remained. Brezovica, with the surrounding hamlets, Staza and Skenderovici, Dimnici, Subin, Osmace, Poznanovici, Podkorjen, and the two hamlets around here, Dedici and Karici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to put the following question to you now. In the course of the month of June 1992, did those villages have any links to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, with the help of the map, why those villages and especially your village of Poznanovici were cut off from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was because of the powerful Serb stronghold at Fakovici which I've marked here on the map. The same goes for Brezani. There were lots of soldiers there who moved around this area, Ratkovici, Fakovici, Ducici, on a daily basis across the Metaljka-Korijen in the direction of Brezani. So that's why we were cut off from Osmace, Mocevici Skenderovici, and Srebrenica in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it risky to move around in that area at all, that is to say for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. All Muslims who tried to cross over and go to one of the enclaves, as I would call them, were either killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your assessment, how far is the area of Ratkovici and Poznanovici from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: More than 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, have I understood you correctly in that you said that those Muslim villages were also isolated from one another in the month of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Every individual village was an enclave in itself and they had to fight for their own survival.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to clarify one point with the witness. I actually asked the question about June, not July. So Mr. Ramic did you understand me correctly? My question to you was whether those villages in the month of June 1992 were isolated from one another.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Ramic, could you please describe briefly to the Trial Chamber the situation in your village of Poznanovici, including the Podkorjen, Dedici, Karici hamlets in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The situation was serious. I said earlier that just in my house there were over 40 people. In view of the fact that this area had about 100 households, then you can check how many homeless people there were. The situation was very serious, chaotic. There was a shortage of food, clothing, medicines. There were no doctors. It was a very, very serious situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Despite this difficult humanitarian situation, were there any other problems?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The other problem was that there were infantry and artillery attacks on a daily basis against the enclaves in order that we are expelled from that area. Every day, refugees, people, civilians, were killed, wounded. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were -- was Poznanovici itself attacked?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, these people who were with you, you said that there were thousands of them. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, thousands.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they try to do anything to get some food?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every day, refugees would try to go to the nearby Muslim village, Zanjevo, Jagovici [phoen] near Fakovici, because it was a place that had a lot of food. They would sneak out there during the night in order to get food so that many of them were killed and wounded on their way to get food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why were they killed?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Because Serbian forces, as I said, were very strong in Fakovici. That area was mined. And simply whether they noticed that somebody was coming to get food, they would fire from their artillery weapons at those civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there ambushes?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The most dangerous were the ambushes set up to trap those civilians who were going to get food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were these ambushes placed?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were located around Ratkovici and Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How far is Fakovici from your village?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I would now like to ask you something else. In Podkorjen and that whole area of Poznanovici, did you have any interest in monitoring the situations in nearby Serb villages, if anything was going on there?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were interested in monitoring that area. We wanted to know what was going on in those villages along the Drina. We knew that people were expelled and that it was our turn, and we would send boys to the guy and Stub A elevations to monitor the movements of the Serb army on the Brezani-Fakovici road, and they knew exactly what was happening and they would tell us when there was a movement of soldiers and where the shelling was coming from and that it was from Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did they tell you about the movements of the Serb military?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: They said that they noticed movements by the Serb army. They were there with horses that were loaded and they were transferring weapons to Brezani.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to Fakovici, did they tell you anything? Did they notice any troop movements along the road between Ratkovici and Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I said earlier that they noticed every day movements of soldiers from Fakovici towards Ratkovici, Branjesovici [phoen], Ducici, and Metaljka-Korjen, Brezani.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also explain to the Trial Chamber at the same time how you were armed in Podkorjen and Poznanovici? First of all, in Podkorjen where you lived. I don't mean you personally. I'm just thinking of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: In Podkorjen and Poznanovici already said we only had five or six hunting rifles. We also had some hand-manufactured pistols and rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how you made these weapons?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a wooden butt to which we would attach a metal barrel and then we would improvise the trigger and the result was that we never knew when firing from such a weapon if it would fire to the front or to the back, and if people would be injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any injuries as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases when people were injured using these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that there was shelling of your area in May and June 1992. Could you please tell us a little bit more about this shelling? Was it frequent or not, and what were the consequences?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every day during May and April, there was artillery shelling and there were also infantry attacks so that many people were wounded and killed by those shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any military facilities in your village in that period?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. They knew exactly that they were shelling civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Ramic, with this mass of refugees that you had that you mentioned, in the -- in early June 1992, was it -- was there any place that you could go to?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. There was no place we could go to. I said that we were an enclave surrounded by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you decide to put up a resistance?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We decided to organise ourselves on a voluntary basis with the weapons that we had at our disposal. We believed that the most prominent teacher amongst us, Dzevad Malkic, who was very respected, he was a good man, calm man, an intelligent man, so we believed him to be the cleverest amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said you had served your military term of duty and you knew what military units were. This group of people that had gathered, at the time, was that a military unit according to what you know about military units?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. It could not have been a military unit because, as I said before, we didn't have adequate weapons, no uniforms, no ammunition, no logistics. So you couldn't really consider that to be a military formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the area of Poznanovici in June 1992, have any communications with other TO units of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, we did not. As I said before, these roads, if one tried to cross them, they would be wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now show the witness P79, Prosecution exhibit. P73 of the 25th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've seen this document before. I showed it to you.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, could you look at the part of the decision, and then you can see under 2, it says, "The following people are appointed to the Srebrenica TO staff, Naser Oric, Atif Ustic, Zulfo Tursunovic, Hamdija Fejzic, Sevket Dozic, Becir Bogilovic, and Ahmo Tihic," and my question to you is: Did you, in June 1992, or at all, were you close to Dzevad Malkic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This group of people, about which you said was -- that was close to him personally, or actually, this group of people around him, including you, did he inform you as a group about the situation in the field?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, on the 25th of May 1992, in Podkorjen and Poznanovici, were you informed about the meeting in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were any of you present at this meeting? Did you ever hear about it?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, nobody attended it. We would -- or I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During May and June 1992, did you know about the existence of any kind of command in Srebrenica? Did you know what it was called?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't know about any command and I wouldn't consider Dzevad Malkic to be a commander at the time in that situation. He was not able to command anyone or order anyone to defend themselves. It was all on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to this but could you please look at the document? Could you look at item 7, which refers to Ahmo Tihic? It states, "Ahmo Tihic from Lijesce is a member of the Srebrenica TO staff, an outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Skelani." Please, please, how can you comment this part of the document referring to Ahmo Tihic? And is it true what it says here, "a prominent activist or outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Skelani." How would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: That is not true because earlier I said that the area of Skelani fell without resistance. They were expelled and Ahmo Tihic was the organiser of that uprising or that resistance. They actually just left Skelani without putting up any resistance. They were expelled. They were wandering around the forest looking for shelter in some villages and also looking for shelter in the forest. They were not organised to put up a resistance then or later, at any point during the summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After June 1992, did you have the opportunity --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Madam Vidovic. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not objecting but it's just a question of clarification. It says the witness answered, "they were expelled and Ahmo Tihic was the organiser of that uprising or that resistance," and then he went on too say they just left Skelani without putting up any resistance. I don't know if it's a problem in the transcript, but the witness has contradicted himself in the space of one answer. So perhaps that need clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I agree with you Mr. Di Fazio. What was -- yes, Madam Vidovic. You put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would say and I thank the Prosecutor, yes, it is a contradiction in the transcript, the witness said that there was no armed resistance so, Witness, could you please clarify that answer.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I meant this decision where it says that Tihic, Ahmo, from Lijesce was a member of the TO and was an activist in armed resistance. That's what I was thinking, that this decision was not true, they were actually expelled and there was no resistance. They were walking around in the woods looking for shelter in some villages. There was no organisation then or at any time later during the summer so it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't answer one area. Was Ahmo Tihic, however, one of the leaders of the Muslims in the Skelani area or not? Was he organising the Muslims, at least in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's what we wanted to know. Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, when you said that he did not organise the Muslims, were you thinking about this period that you are talking about, the spring and summer, not the whole war?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said in that period, and in the course of the summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just wanted to be quite clear about this, Your Honours. My next question, Mr. Ramic, is: After June 1992, did you have the opportunity to talk to people from Mocevici? After June 1992.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. After June, much later, I did have the opportunity to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This decision that you just looked at, was there anyone there who could possibly cover the area of Mocevici in May and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Vekaz Husic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After June 1992, did you have the opportunity to speak with him?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to speak to him after June, about the situation. He told me that they also had suffered a number of artillery and infantry attacks from Ratkovici, meaning that the young men who were reconnoitering at the elevation, they saw that Mocevici were being hit by mortars from Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In these conversations you had with Mr. Vekaz Husic, was a command or the command in Srebrenica ever mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. No command was mentioned. As I said, there was no command. I mentioned Dzevad. Nobody was in a position to command where we were. It was more of a voluntary setup so nobody could make an order for anyone to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he share with you any of his information about a command in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how far Mocevici is from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like the usher to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit P75. The decision by the TO of Srebrenica from the 26th of May 1992. It's 3/92. Witness, you've seen this decision, I showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to look at these names. I am going to read the text behind these two names, Krdzic, Atif from Srebrenica is a member of the TO Staff from Srebrenica; organiser of armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Osmace, Nedzad Bektic from Karacici is a member of the Srebrenica TO Staff organiser of armed resistance in the area of Kragljivoda; Senahid Tabakovic from Bratunac is a member of the Srebrenica TO staff, one of the organisers of armed resistance in the area of Skenderovici, and first of all I would like to ask you if in June 1992 you had contacts with any of these people, Krdzic, Atif, Bektic, Nedzad, and Tabakovic, Senahid?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any contacts then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Did you consider any of them to be your commander in Poznanovici at the time?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, not then and not later at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How far is Osmace from your area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Kragljivoda?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Skenderovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: About 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Nedzad Bektic and, if you did know him, did you speak with him after June 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him and we talked together after the fall of Brezani.
