utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you to look at item 2 of this decision again, which states that the staff is expanded and that Nedzad Bektic will be part of it as an organiser of armed resistance in the area of Kragljivoda. How can you comment on this? Was Nedzad Bektic really the organiser of armed resistance in that area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, that is not true. Later, I said that I talked to Nedzad Bektic after the fall of Brezani, and he was -- he had attended the military academy in Belgrade, and that precisely at that time in May he had arrived to the Bratunac area from Belgrade, and he was lucky to avoid being arrested in Bratunac, and he managed to come to the Srebrenica area villages in the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know and to what he said, was he an organiser of the armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. He was not because people did not really accept him gladly in that area because he had come directly from the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out who organised resistance in the area of Kragljivoda?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later I found out that the leader and organiser of the group at Kragljivoda was Sefik Mandic, until he was killed in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you think then that this -- what is stated in this document is true? Is it true what it says in this document?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. I apologise to the interpreters. Mr. Ramic, again I would like to ask you that after I finish my question, then you make a short break or you make a pause before you give your answer. You described attacks on your village in the course of June 1992, and you said that the shelling came from Ratkovici. What -- on what basis do you claim that the shelling came from the direction of Ratkovici in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Unless I misunderstood the evidence, if Your Honours please, I thought the witness had answered this question, has already given evidence about the boys who went up on to the hill. Now, perhaps I misunderstood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did say before that they were sending the boys up to the school or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Up to the elevation area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He gave two names. If you look at it somewhere, I've lost it of course, it was Gaj and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are right. I think he has answered this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not objecting of course if Madam Vidovic can lead more evidence about it but for it to be comprehensible it's got to be understood in the context of the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Di Fazio. However you may proceed if you want to elicit more information on the matter, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's exactly what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned the shelling and you said that it came from the direction of Ratkovici and you mentioned the boys, these boys and certain men. Did these people have anything with them that would help them to monitor the situation?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had binoculars that they had borrowed from the hunters, from those elevations, perhaps I said that, and perhaps I didn't, from the Gaj and Stub A elevations you could see the Ratkovici area and Ducici with the naked eye and with binoculars you could really see 100 per cent that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you mentioned the location of Gaj above Dedici. What can you see from there?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I said earlier that you could see villages, the villages of Ratkovici, and you could see exactly where the shooting was coming from and where our area, the area of Mocevici was being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This will help us. This will be an exhibit, the Prosecution Exhibit P356 [as interpreted]. We will be looking at some other documents in regard of these events but I would now like the usher to show the witness P376. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, I heard you say 356 before. Is it a mistake, Ms. Vidovic you meant 376? At least in the -- when I say "I heard you say," I heard the interpreter say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 376, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in any case, I meant P376.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now I understood that but I wanted to make sure because the transcript said 356.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a blown-up area of Ratkovici, Ducice, and Poznanovici. Mr. Ramic, I would like you to look at this map and to show the area of Ratkovici once again for the Trial Chamber. Don't make any markings on the map, just point with your hand.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: [Witness points]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness points at the spot on the map P376, on a spot shown as Ratkovici, or marked as Ratkovici. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please point to Poznanovici and Podkorjen once again for us? And Podkorjen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's Podkorjen. It's further down, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map actually ends at Podkorjen and the witness is indicating that it's that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please slow us Stub A again on this map that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to mark it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, just point it out for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the witness indicates a spot at 11.00 above Poznanovici as being Stup A. Yes, thank you. Let's move. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you see the altitudes of this map of Ratkovici and Poznanovici, and could you tell us what the altitude is?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Somewhere around here you could see that Ratkovici is at 442 above sea level and Poznanovici is a little bit to the east, 376, somewhere around Mlecva so that if we go to the west, then you could see that the altitude is also approximately 440 metres above sea level. So the altitude of Ratkovici and Poznanovici is more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you mentioned that the artillery attacks came from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What do you state that, on what -- on which basis are you stating that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: We knew where Fakovici was and which direction it lay in. However, I said in the beginning that there were thousands of refugees in my village and there were a lot of refugees from Zanjevo and another village and we would go at the request of these people to their houses and bring food back in the evening and we would pass above Fakovici, and we could see that they had mortars in Fakovici, that they also had antiaircraft guns and antiaircraft cannon, and when people were going into Abdulici, they would be firing from these weapons at these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see and experience that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I personally saw and experienced that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned that the artillery shooting came from some other directions. Did it come from the Skelani area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it came from the direction of Jezero. We knew exactly that there were mortars at Jezero, and the refugees who used to come from those areas told us Sabica [phoen] and Ahmo, who came from Skelani, said that there were mortars at Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they told us and they said that they saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell the Trial Chamber now whether anything specific happened in your village on the 8th of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 8th of June 1992, it was a Monday, and the Serbs cut off electricity for our villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards on that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: After that, there was a powerful artillery and infantry attack at Podkorjen and Podrevici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: It came from Ratkovici and from Ducici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that Ratkovici and Ducici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Because, as I said, we had boys who were observing all that. You could see it with the naked eye but they had binoculars and they could tell exactly where the attack was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, how far did those units come on that day? Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, the units came to Podkorjen, the road called Metaljak going to Podkorjen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I think there might be a slight mischaracterisation of the witness's testimony. I think he testified that there was artillery coming. I haven't heard him testifying yet as to units coming. So if that could just be clarified or else I think we might be misleading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. That's a very valid comment. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecutor may have misunderstood because the witness answered in 11.32, "afterwards there was a powerful artillery and infantry attack."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have I interpreted your comment correctly?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much to the witness. And now could we go back to my previous question I asked you, about how far Metaljka was from Podkorjen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: About 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At what time of the day did this happen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: At noon, at mid-day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the 8th of June 1992, at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Do you remember specifically any one of those observers that you talked to, any one of the people who were looking at it?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember a boy called Hamid Smajlovic who informed us that the Serb army was moving from the direction of Fakovici, Ratkovici and Ducici, and that they had already come as far as Metaljka.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you in what way they were moving?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were armed and they had horses for the transport of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were they surrounding you or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told us that the Serb army was attacking Poznanovici from the direction of Ratkovici at the same time. I talked to Dzevad at the time as well so basically the Serbs were surrounding us in a semi-circle, and so there was no way out except in the direction of Fakovici and we knew that it was a Serb stronghold that that the road was mined.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did that boy, who you talked to, mention any murders? Did he mention having seen any murders?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the road to Podkorjen the Serbs killed Osmanovic Kadrija from Podkorjen, and another person --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make it clear that I don't -- I'm not stopping Madam Vidovic when she puts leading questions unless I hear an objection from you. That's the understanding. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer my question? The young man that you talked to, did he mention any murders of anyone?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did say he mentioned the murder of Kadrija Osmanovic from Podkorjen and a man called Refik from Josevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do apologise. You have already answered that question. And what did you do when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, we resolved to get organised, to organise the weapons that we had and to go out to Metaljka to wait for the Serb forces in order to give the opportunity to the inhabitants, that is to flee to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, the population managed to get to the woods and we managed to surprise the Serbs by going out to meet them at Metaljka and there was fierce fighting there and the Serbs were somewhat surprised, the Serb military were surprised, and they had to withdraw again in the direction of Ratkovici and a number of other villages in the direction of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that one-to-one fight, were you had -- at close quarters?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice what sort of weapons they had if they had any?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we noticed that they had automatic rifles, machine-guns, machine-gun, calibre 84, and it was the first time I saw it in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the uniforms on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had camouflage uniforms, olive-grey colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, after that, after things died down a little bit, did you search the area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We continued searching the area because we had quite a few wounded in that battle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you find anything?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We found a lot of ammunition, which was actually precious to us afterwards as a logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find any bodies?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whilst searching the area we found the body of Ognjen Markovic, called Bato, at Metaljka there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to show the witness the document D45. It is a list of those killed from the area of Bratunac between 1992 and 1996. And could you please look on page 9, number 298. It is also on page 8 in the English version -- 9, sorry, in the English version. You've seen this document, Witness, right? Can you check the name 298, Markovic, Andrija, Ognjen, born on the 20th - sorry - of December 1950 from Fakovici, and the date of his death is the 8th of June 1992, at the village Podkorjen. And in relation to this document I'm going to put the following question to you. Is that indeed the person who was killed during the attack on your village that you've just described to us?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's the person who was killed on that occasion on Podkorjen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us that you knew him. And can you tell us now how far is the place of his death from his own house?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: About 16 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, did you see his dead body?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was he wearing on that occasion, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I can remember it quite clearly. He was wearing camouflage uniform, bullet-proof vest and automatic rifle and a quite a few bombs and ammunition, a lot of ammunition, incendiary bombs and fragmentation ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if anything happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the next three days and nights, fierce artillery attacks continued pounding our villages and civilian population, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the shelling coming from?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: It came exactly from Ratkovici, Magdovici and Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if anyone was looking for that body?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of June, 1992, I remember clearly because I saw lots of Serb soldiers who came back to Metaljka on that day and they were searching the area and they were looking for their comrades in arms, their dead bodies, and on that occasion they killed a young boy from Mocevici and I found out about that later, from Vekaz, who came to us to ask for assistance for Mocevici and he could see that the artillery from Ratkovici was attacking Mocevici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out whether the infantry from Ratkovici or any other surrounding villages were also attacking Mocevici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the infantry was launching attacks as well. I said that there request quite a few soldiers at Metaljka that day. I saw those soldiers. I was really very close. And I myself witnessed the killing of that young boy. Afterwards, they blew his body up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you the following. Did you ever find out whether on that day, on the 10th of June 1992, there was an infantry attack against Mocevici as well?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I found out later on when we later talked to Vekaz. He told me that they were subjected to fierce artillery and infantry attacks from Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the 10th of June, after that, were there any other attacks on your area, your villages, Poznanovici and Podkorjen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th of June, I remember very clearly it was a Friday, there was another powerful artillery and infantry attack from Ratkovici and they entered Poznanovici and they managed to set 80 per cent of the village on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell me who attacked your village on that occasion, do you know?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: We knew exactly that those were people from Ratkovici and Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ramic. Could you slow down, please? On the basis of what did you know that those people were from Ratkovici? What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, after the withdrawal of the Serb army from Poznanovici, we got to Poznanovici to get out the wounded or perhaps the dead bodies, and to bury the bodies. And then we find out from Abdulah Halilovic from Poznanovici that he himself witnessed the murder of his daughter-in-law, who was heavily pregnant, because they were not far from those attacking Serb soldiers. His son was wounded in both legs and his daughter-in-law was killed and Abdulah Hanura [phoen] managed to hide a little bit further away and so they actually recognised their neighbours from Ratkovici, Fakovici, who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from those people, that you mentioned, they were in the fields and they were working in the fields, were any other people killed in Poznanovici on that day?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: All those who didn't manage to leave Poznanovici, to run away, were either killed or murdered.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, as far as you were concerned, did things worsen for you after the 12th of June 1992 or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation got a lot worse. Perhaps that was the most difficult period that I can remember. And at that time -- could I have a break, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We are going to have a break in 12 minutes' time. We will have it now. Can I suggest, Madam Vidovic, I just want to make sure that you will be able to finish your examination-in-chief if I give the witness 30 minutes' break. In other words, you will have an hour and a half, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour, I'm convinced I'll be able to make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will resume -- let's say we will resume at 15 minutes past 12. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just before we continue, Madam Vidovic and Madam Sellers and Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Jones, I just had a phone call Judge Eser. There is no way he's going to turn up this week. So just to put you on notice that the situation has crystallised in a way that he doesn't even need my suggestion to stay there. He has decided to stay there. All right? Also, on -- because he's needed there. I don't want to be misunderstood that this is something -- so are you feeling better, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the day when everyone is not feeling well. So we have to cope with the situation. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, we stopped when I asked you whether the situation worsened in any way for you after the 12th of June, and you replied it did. And that it was one of the hardest periods of your life. Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber why it was like that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that there were thousands of refugees in our area, Poznanovici, Podkorjen, Dedici, and Karici, and when the Serb army came into Poznanovici and destroyed the village, the entire population from the area had to leave, together with all the other refugees who were already there in those villages, and they set out but they had nowhere to go. I said that we were surrounded. So the only possibility was to hide in a nearby forest near Podkorjen which was called Poljana --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ramic, we will come to that. Could you show the Trial Chamber this area, Poljana? Do you still have the map? Could you perhaps leave the map with the witness until the end. If you have the map, I think it's P376 that we had earlier on, P376. Mr. Ramic, could you locate the area of Poljana on that map? That forest, I mean.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I can't on this map. I need another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You've got the other map underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Shouldn't we mention the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. This is D721, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you point it again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if you have a pencil, could you mark an X there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another letter because we have already got Xs. With a P, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And can you explain to the Trial Chamber, can you describe how many people were there and what was their condition?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the entire population was there, with the refugees. Thousands of them. And there was this exodus of this entire population, and they all went to that forest called Poljana and they had no where else to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting but can I ask you about -- does that group include the inhabitants of your village, Podkorjen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it was Poznanovici, Karici, Dedici and Podkorjen and all the refugees who were staying at those villages as well. The locals and the refugees. And they all went up to the forest called Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Poljana and we were being shelled and we were subjected to infantry attacks as well. The people had no where else to go so they went into the forest called Poljana.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did that mean that they were all outdoors?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all outdoors and that referred to the elderly, women and children, and there was no medical care, we had no medicines of any kind, no doctors, we had no facilities of any sort. People were building shacks with branches and dead wood, and the wind would blow it all away and it was almost as if the heavens had turned against us as well because it rained incessantly for 10 days. There was no food. We didn't have enough clothes and we were under attack and we had to make do. We had to eat mushrooms in the forest because we had nothing else, and that's why I find it particularly hard to talk about this. And my children, I've got three children, and they were in the forest as well with my parents, and women were having children. Mrs. Smajlovic had a baby in that forest and it is something which is simply inconceivable for the civilised world today.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understood you correctly when you said that prior to the 12th of June 1992, thousands of people had been outdoors?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Thousands of people for 10 days, yes, yes, it's true for 10 days, they were outdoors and they were subjected to incessant artillery attacks, to rain and adverse weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what went on in the early morning hours on the 21st of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 21st of June, the most severe combined artillery and infantry attack by the Serb forces from Ratkovici actually started.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you react to that attack?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, simply, and this is something I've mentioned on a number of occasions, these people had nowhere to go. We were surrounded and a group of us who had some weapons decided that we should defend ourselves, and if the Serbs came into the woods, they would massacre the population. They would probably start killing and raping people so we decided to stand up to them and to perhaps even lose our lives, but try and put a stop to the kind of suffering that the other villages along the river had experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, we set out to meet them, with what weapons we had. We no longer paid any heed to the situation. We had the weapons that we could. We didn't care whether we were killed or not. We decided that we would rather all be killed but we had to stop the Serbs getting to the people and at one point I heard some noise. I turned around and I could see that masses of people -- well, they were almost going mad, they followed us, whoever could walk followed, even though we did tell them not to. Dzevad Markic [phoen] was shouting at them not to, but they had nowhere else to go and so it was all or nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when did that happen? What was the time of day?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, it took place on the 21st of June 1992, at around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to see the Serb forces coming close to you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did see the Serbs coming close, but we had no choice. The people were walking behind us and there was no way we could stop them. It was not possible to control the people any more. They were just walking, they carried whatever they could. They were carrying axes, saws, they were taking pots and pans, banging on them. It was just a terrible sight. As I said, the people were almost crazed. They had gone mad.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did this have any effect on the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the Serb soldiers were approaching, when they saw this mass of people, they simply started to withdraw, to run away, to throw down their weapons, which at that point we found. I saw a machine-gun, an automatic rifle, a semi-automatic rifle. I could see also some shells, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how far did you get to?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I got to Gornji Ratkovici, close to Gornji Ratkovici. At that point, I couldn't continue because there was fire from a machine-gun from the houses, automatic weapons' fire from the houses so we couldn't approach the villages. They were firing at us. We were firing at them. I said that I had a pistol with me at the time. Simply, at the time, we just couldn't get any closer. They were firing mostly from the houses. There were also some trenches but it was from trenches that were about 15 metres from the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point did the Serbs withdraw? What happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: After a while they pulled back towards Grabovicka Rijeka [phoen], and Fakovici. During the withdrawal of the Serb forces, we entered the village and that's when we found very quickly the weapons, machine-gun, automatic and semi-automatic weapons, a mortar. I found a mortar. I myself found one. I saw that there was one in the village. There were many mortar shells in the village that had been fired from that mortar so that we gathered those weapons very quickly and then we had to go back as quickly as possible to our villages because we were afraid of a counterattack, and an attack from the direction of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just a clarification, if Your Honours please. I wonder if the witness is talking about Grabovici or Fakovici when he said he went into the village and found this weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, you need to explain or clarify this, Mr. Ramic. What was the name of the village where you entered and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gornji Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it, if you follow line 22 on page 62. But anyway, it's clear now. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You talked about the Serbs who were withdrawing towards Grabovicka Rijeka and Fakovici is that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to show the witness a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you see the document, Mr. Ramic, can I just ask you, you said that you found a mortar yourself. Where did you find it?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: We found a mortar in a barn. The other one, another one was in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now look at document -- it's a document from the Drina Corps command of the 14th of December -- November 1992. It's a combat report, ERN number 04268306.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the last paragraph of the document? I showed you this document, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read the last part of the report. "A five-year-old boy was killed in the area of responsibility of the 3rd PLBR, the cause of death is the boy's carelessness as he was playing near a 25-millimetre antiaircraft cannon which triggered off and killed him." I would like to remind you, Mr. Ramic, that you mentioned Brezovica. Let me just clarify one thing. Is the village of Brezovica -- were there any Serb hamlets in that area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the village of Barice.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Although this document is dated November 1992, in relation to this boy who was killed playing with an antiaircraft cannon, I would like to ask you the following. Are you surprised by this note in the report that a PAT antiaircraft cannon was accessible to this five-year-old boy, in view of the experience you had with weapons in Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't surprising. We knew that had he had so many weapons that even children were playing with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Ramic, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what a PAT is?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: A PAT is an antiaircraft cannon, [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Madam Vidovic. This document which consists of one page in the B/C/S version and two pages in the English version is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D723. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, again I would like to take you back to the events of the 21st of June 1992. At the time, when you were with this group of armed people in Ratkovici, did you see anything burning?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could see a barn in Brdjani, it's a part belonging to Gornji Ratkovici. I could see it burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were any houses burning in Ratkovici at the time?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the houses burning at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you withdrew from Ratkovici, did the other armed people withdraw together with you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they all quickly withdrew with us. We ran back quickly to our positions expecting an attack from Fakovici at our villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, the people from your villages, Podkorjen and Poznanovici, have any interest in setting these houses on fire? Did you have an interest in doing something like that, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. We had no interest in torching those houses because we had so many people without homes whom we wanted to accommodate in those homes and Dzevad always said not to destroy this property, that we were not like the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you left the armed soldiers [as interpreted] of the -- of that area, what happened to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: The civilians stayed in the villages looking for food. They mostly came to those villages looking for food. So they couldn't return immediately. So at the time, we did not follow what was happening with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I was asking the question, I said "armed persons." I didn't say armed soldiers, as it is stated in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you, Mr. Ramic, didn't I, that after these armed persons left, and not soldiers --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So at one point you told us that you were afraid of a counterattack from Fakovici. Were you afraid of an encounter attack from anywhere else on that day, the 21st of June?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: From Fakovici, yes, and from Ratkovici, Vranesevici, from up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Vranesevici. And were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: And also the shelling went on from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how many -- how far Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it in a time frame. I mean, we are talking of post 21st of June of 1992 but until when did they -- because he describes it as an ongoing -- sort of an ongoing shelling. Until what period of time, until when, did this shelling continue, shelling from Serbia continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I asked the witness about the 21st. We are still talking about the 21st. And then later we will. So now I'm asking him --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Ramic, did you -- you mentioned Serbia. Were you afraid, did the danger come from there also or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: They had artillery support from Serbia, the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. And finally, on that day, on the 21st of June 1992, was there a counter attack by the Serbs against you after all this you described?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could you please clarify this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That day, the 21st of June, after you with drew and you said that the civilians stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a counter attack on that area including those civilians there who were in Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a counterattack, artillery counterattack. There was firing from Fakovici and Magdovici. They knew that they were shooting at civilians because the civilians were in those villages looking for food so that they intensely shelled the civilians, wounding them and destroying their own houses. Both Serb and Muslim houses were destroyed in this artillery attack. They were shooting non-discriminately.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Mr. Ramic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did I see you stand up, Mr. Di Fazio or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I just moved to make a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you described the weapons that you had. Did any of you that day, who were carrying the weapons and took part in the attack, wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, nobody had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If anybody were to claim that the attackers on Ratkovici on that day wore different uniforms, including olive drab, camouflage uniforms, with red and green berets on their heads, would that be true?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You described to us how refugees stayed behind in the villages, in the area of Ratkovici, after the attack. Did you notice what they had with them when they came back to the village, if they were carrying anything?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: They had building materials, windows, and doors, along with the food, in order to improvise some huts where they could stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The more prominent people from Poznanovici and Podkorjen, intellectuals, did you try to speak with these people, these refugees, so that they would try to move into these houses in Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did try to talk with them and talked with them on several occasions. They simply didn't want to do it because the area of Ratkovici was constantly shelled so that it was not safe for them to move into those houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing. If anyone were to claim that before the attack on the 21st of June 1992, there were no organised Serb military units in Ratkovici, that these were just village guards, would that be true?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: It would be absolutely untrue. If they were village guards, where did the machine guns, automatic rifles, snipers, hand-held rocket launchers, etc. come from? 8 Q. Based on your knowledge about the military, do village guards have mortars?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: They don’t have mortars… Village guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that the question emerges now, obvious. But could you repeat your question, please, Madam Vidovic? Because the interpreters failed to get it. What was your question, at least tell me, you just have to make the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My question referred to mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you found mortars there. Did village guards, according to what you know about village guards, have mortars?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MS. VIDOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Another clarification matter so that I can understand the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's not so much mortar. It's who, who's organising the attacks. The witness said -- it was put to the witness that, is it true -- is a claim that there were no organised Serb military units in Ratkovici true? True and the witness then went on to say, "Look it's absolutely untrue." And then in the next line, then the witness -- it appears in the transcript, "No, there were no attacks other than the ones by the village guard."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is what I tried to get Madam Vidovic to explain because the interpreters failed to get the question that Madam Vidovic put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, we are all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, reading the answer given by the witness, one can understand what the question was but I asked Madam Vidovic to tell us what her question was to the witness and she has told us another question which obviously was not the question that she had put to the witness before. So that's the position. If you could clarify this, Madam Vidovic? Let's take it --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said no there were no attacks other than the ones -- I lost it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, Your Honours, Your Honours, I'm speaking very slowly and I'm speaking very clearly. I asked the witness about village guards, if they can -- that what he saw, was that organised, were there organised units in Ratkovici and can it be considered that these were village guards and he very clearly responded that there was -- there were none. I did not ask any question about organised attacks. And the witness did not mention that there were no attacks. My first question was whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The previous question, Madam Vidovic, please, let's not complicate matters. If you go to page 69, line 9, your question was another thing, "If anyone were to claim that before the attack on 21st of June 1992 there were no organised Serb military units in Ratkovici, that there were -- that these were just village guards, would that be true?" And he answered, "It would be absolutely untrue. If they were village guards, only then."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Were these snipers, the hand-held rocket automatic and semi-automatic rifles," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there was a question which the interpreters didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which he answered, "No, there were no attacks other than the ones by the village guards."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly what I tried to explain and then I continued on with my question which referred to whether the witness found a mortar there and I asked him whether village guards had mortars. Neither I nor the witness mentioned this. There were no attacks. At no point did the witness say anything like that. But he responded to my question that village guards had no mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, please, witness, could you correct me in I'm not right, did you talk about any attacks?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, no, I said exactly what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Is it clear enough to you, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's proceed. That is -- solves the problem. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, what happened after the 21st of June 1992, in the entire area of your villages, Poznanovici, Dedici, Podkorjen, and Karici. What happened, including Mocevici, if anything happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: There were fierce artillery attacks in the area of Poznanovici, Ratkovici, and Mocevici, artillery and infantry attacks on the villages so that those villages were practically destroyed. Many people were injured and many people were killed in the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to meet Mr. Vekaz Husic after June, and what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. After June in the summer, I spoke to Vekaz Husic and he told me then that they also had fierce artillery and infantry attacks from the direction of Ratkovici and that they had fights in Ducici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you talked about the attack on the 21st of June 1992 on Ratkovici. Did you then -- I'm thinking of your group which had weapons, and Mr. Malkic -- did you have an order at the time from anyone from Srebrenica about an attack or did you have contacts with anybody from Srebrenica in relation to this event?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any orders from anyone in Srebrenica. I said that this was a spontaneous thing, the situation was what it was and that we had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the event of the 21st of June, did you have any agreements with people from Mocevici, Brezovica, Skenderovici, or Osmace about that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. I said at the beginning I was explaining that these villages were an enclave each. It was not possible to communicate precisely because of the road that -- that Serb road that was passing through Ratkovici, Ducice, Metaljka, Korijan, Brezani, and that many who tried to cross that road were killed or wounded and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the usher to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit P80. This is an alleged document by the staff of the Srebrenica armed forces signed by Nedzad Bektic, and they are talking here about the establishment structure, first formation structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic. Did I show you this document before?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to look at what it states here. In that part 1, first formation structure, look, and it says on the 20th of May 1992, in Bajramovici, a TO Territorial Defence staff was being formed. From 17th of April 1992 to mid-October 1992 the first regional units were formed under -- of a regional character, under the auspices of the TO, namely. And then can you look at what it states under item 3, TO Osmace. It says Tokoljaci company, Osmace company, Poznanovici company, in brackets (A1, AII, AIII), 111 conscripts, commander Dzevad Malkic. And underneath it says the commander of the TO Osmace is Atif-Sakib Krdzic. I would like to now ask you the following question: In the period mentioned here from the 17th of April until mid-October 1992, Mr. Ramic, these armed men from your village that you mentioned today, your group of fighters, people from Poznanovici, was it part of the Osmace TO?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. Not then and not much later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it part of the Osmace TO?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, it was never part of the Osmace TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your commander at any time during the course of the war in 1992, was your commander Sakib Atic [phoen] or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, he was never our commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before October 1992, did you have anything that in military terms would constitute a company of fighters?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. Simply at the beginning like I said, I talked about our weapons and, later, we captured some weapons and perhaps we had ten rifles at the most. We simply didn't have the equipment. We didn't have the ammunition or the logistics in order to be some kind of military unit. We didn't have uniforms. We simply didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say rifles, real rifles, are you thinking of semi-automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Semi-automatic and carbines, and some automatic rifles that we captured later?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you in Poznanovici have 111 as it says here conscripts, soldiers, whatever you wish?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, no way. I said earlier that if we had the weapons and the conscripts, we wouldn't have experienced what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please could you tell the Trial Chamber now, how far Osmace is from where you were?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like you to look at the same document. On page 3, it states, "On the 14th of October 1992, the -- with the order of the commander, the units were reorganised in the following way." So could you please look at next page, page 4, under number 6, it states, "Independent Biljeg battalion based in Biljeg, commander Ahmo Tihic. And then it mentions the first, second, and third and fourth company with the headquarters in Poznanovici, Commander Malkic Dzevad, and I would like to ask you some questions about that. First of all, Mr. Ramic, do you know that in October 1992, was there any kind of reorganisation or restructuring which would possibly place your command -- your unit under the command of somebody from the Biljeg battalion? I'm talking about October 1992.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just trying to follow the evidence. Do you know where in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bottom or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Got it. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, please, did you register that in this first part of the document it says that the Poznanovici company is part of the Osmace TO and then we have Biljeg here. Do you have any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: This comment says that there were no reorganisation of the TO and that it says that it's in Osmace in one place and Biljeg in another place so it means that something here is not quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How far is --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How far is Biljeg from Poznanovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How far?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: 8 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Eight kilometres. And let's just clarify the transcript a little bit, please. What it states here about Poznanovici belonging, that unit that was there, belonging to either Biljeg or Osmace in the period of 1992, October 1992, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: It's completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- actually, when did you actually start to use the word "battalion" for your fighters? Do you know whether this happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: This happened after the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. So this was sometime in early 1994 when they were talking about us belonging to the Biljeg Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, do you know that towards the end of the war you were registered as belonging to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the war, we were registered as belonging to Skenderovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber why you say "on paper." You mentioned demilitarisation. What did demilitarisation mean to you? Can you explain the Trial Chamber what the situation was like and can you please wait for my question to be interpreted, which now it has been.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, demilitarisation meant that the weapons that we had in our possession, those few weapons, we had to relinquish them to the international forces which were in Srebrenica. So basically those weapons had been destroyed. So at that time we were not allowed to own or carry arms because arms would be taken away from us. The only possibility was for somebody to have it hidden away somewhere. In that case they would have kept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After demilitarisation, in that protected area, could you engage in any military activity at all?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No we couldn't. I said that the weapons had been relinquished.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And for those battalions or brigades or whatever did they ever function in any way?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, no. As I said it was only in existence on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask the usher to show another exhibit to the witness. It's P95. I would like you to take a look at page 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this part is on page 12, the second half of item 3 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please look at page 16, Witness? I've shown you this document before, right?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to quote from a part of the text on page 16 which reads, "On 26th [as interpreted] of June 1992, in coordination with the Territorial Defence Bilje, Territorial Defence Skenderovici, Territorial Defence Osmace, and Territorial Defence Srebrenica, the Chetniks were expelled from the strongpoint, Ratkovici, Polimci, Ducici, Dvorista, and Brdjani, when the larger war trophy consisting of weapons and food was obtained." Now, on the basis of your experience on -- on the basis of what you yourself saw on the 21st of June 1992, can you tell us whether in the course of that battle at Ratkovici you saw any of those units participating there?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. There was no joint attack. It was just a spontaneous response to this fierce attack from the Serbs and I said that there were lots of refugees from a number of villages and everybody went there in order to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you this. Do you know Mr. Senahid Tabakovic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when I talk about you, I mean the unit at Poznanovici. So in the periods of time up until the fall of 1992, had he ever been any -- in any sort of a commanding position with regard to you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, not then and not much later either.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So we are talking about that same period of time in 1992 and I would like to know whether at any point he appeared in the area of your village?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. And I want to ask you something else, Mr. Ramic. After the events in June 1992, did you yourself ever had the opportunity to see the area of Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to see that area. I went to those villages and I saw that --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, just a moment. If anyone were to claim that the houses in Ratkovici in the month of June 1992 were burnt to the ground, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until September 1992, would that claim be correct? I mean, did you see those houses in the period of time prior to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And the houses had not been burned down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what went on in that area in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Let me just stress, Your Honours, that the shelling and the artillery attacks took place on a daily basis and as of September, it continued, those artillery attacks continued, and they were even more powerful, and so, as I said, they were shelling with no regard as to whether those were Serb or Muslim villages because there would be civilians there looking for food. So they were shelling everyone and everything at that time. At that time, at some point in September, there was a fierce bombing by planes in the area of Srebrenica, and what I mean is our villages, Srebrenica and the Serb villages, so various types of bombs were being dropped on the area, and most of those villages had already been destroyed at that time, and most of those houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether those Serb attacks on your area went on through the autumn and the winter of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were continued in the autumn and the winter, and on the 26th of January 1993, up until the end of March 1993, that was probably the period of the most fierce artillery attacks in that area. They were shelling the entire area. Let me try and explain this a little bit better. It was all the villages, even the Serb villages where the Muslims were, every inch of the land was being shelled so there was no way to hide anywhere. We tried to offer resistance, as much as we could, but in the end we had to withdraw all the way to Srebrenica. And what I mean here is both shelling and the infantry attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So do you have any knowledge about whether that shelling affected -- that kind of shelling affected the village of Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I mean, I was there. I saw it myself. I could see shells landing on houses, destroying houses. The houses were disappearing and I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like the usher to show another exhibit to the witness. It is a document coming from the Bratunac Brigade dated the 1st of April 1993, and I would just like you to take a look at this document. In item 1 the reference is to the battles in the area of Pirici and Ratkovici. And can you please look at the last bit of text in item 1? Item 2, sorry, and I'm going to quote it to you. "On the brigade's left wings the second PB infantry battalion and the Mauzer Brigade attacked along the Sikirici-Mocevici axis in the Hrstovice and Kluvci village sector. The fifth PB was active in the Ratkovici village sector. Can we say that this document confirms the attacks that you mentioned earlier, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This confirms exactly those attacks, that is to say action from Fakovici when they took Fakovici again, so they were shelling the areas that I described before, and they destroyed houses in Ratkovici and in Poznanovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. We will give this document an exhibit number. It will become Defence Exhibit D724. For the record it consists of two pages, one in B/C/S, and the other one the corresponding English translation. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've been trying to follow the evidence of this witness with some success, I think. I thought he was describing events in 1992 around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because he moved into -- because he was asked by Madam Vidovic how this progressed over time. And he went into practically April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I -- of course, if you would like any clarifications, you are entitled to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll reserve it for tomorrow to clarify it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To me, at least, I only speak for myself, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have been able to follow. It started off with the demilitarisation and it ended up basically the happenings, the events between June of 1992 and continuing attacks going into April of 1993. So this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I apologise for any interruption in the flow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I would ask that if we could be just a little more clearer, if the witness is describing -- also for the purposes of the transcript if I've misunderstood I'll clarify it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly, may I respond to this? I asked the following question: I asked whether the attacks continued throughout the fall and winter, and whether they went on between the 26th of January in 1993 and the end of March 1993. So it was crystal clear. And the witness understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was the winter and spring. I think we are wasting time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Yes, I'd like to ask the usher to show yet another exhibit to the witness. It is about the subsequent attacks. Once again, it is Exhibit D51, the document D51. It's a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the document, Witness? I've shown it to you before, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a Bratunac Brigade document dated the 19th of April 1993 and I'm just going to quote the relevant bit out to you which is on page 3 of this document. It reads, in item 5(5), and it's again on page 3 in the English text, it says, "From the initial position TT.651 - TT.322" or rather "Ratkovici-Ducici, the 5th Infantry Battalion, and TG.G-1 attack the enemy in the zone of: Magudovic Brdo [800 metres to the north] - Oparci - Kulici - Dimnici - Mocevici - Subin. "The main activity direction: Magudovic Brdo [TT651] - Grada [TT.726] - Mocevici - Stozersko." And, "Support to be provided by Brigade AG of the Bratunac Brigade. Command spot at the village of Ratkovici -- command spot, that is in the village of Ratkovici." And my question to you, Mr. Ramic, is whether Magudovic - Brdo is a part of Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document illustrate what you were talking about, the fact that artillery attacks were being launched against the Magudovic - Brdo by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Could you -- no, we already have a number for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, now we are going to move on to an altogether different topic. May we just go back to the summer of 1992, since I'm going to ask you something about a different location? What about the overall situation in the entire area, Poznanovici and a wider area as well? Did it worsen in any way in the course of the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It got worse because as I mentioned on a number of occasions, thousands and thousands of refugees came to the area and they had no food and we were subjected to shelling on a daily basis and they had to go to other villages, Abdulici, near Fakovici, to find food in the course of the night and many stepped on mines or there were ambushes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you about is the following. What is the significance of Fakovici, if any, in as far as this shelling in the course of the summer of 1992 is concerned?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew that significant Serb forces were stationed at Fakovici, that there were lots of soldiers, and an uncle of mine mentioned that in April he came from Cacak across Pacavaci [phoen], and he saw large numbers of Serb soldiers and he saw the artillery weapons in Fakovici and he saw lots of uniformed Serb soldiers and their weapons, and he saw all that in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they shell your area in the course of the summer from Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your account here, you mentioned that your uncle in the month of April went through Bacevci and Fakovici. Could you just tell us for the sake of the transcript, in April of what year?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: April 1992, the beginning, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned those refugees from Fakovici and let me try and make the long story short, or, rather, from the area of Abdulici. I do apologise. Do you remember whether you went looking for food with them in the course of the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. We had quite a few refugees from Abdulici and Zanjevo. I had a name called Ibrahim in my house, and on a number of occasions we gave him -- or rather we went to Abdulici and Zanjevo and we had a horse with us. And they used to be wealthy. They had lots of grain so we would go and collect food there and then we would come back, but as I've already mentioned on their way to collect food many people lost their lives or were wounded and it was easy to see that they had an antiaircraft gun and -- at Fakovici, and they could use it against us when we were looking for food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to ask you a specific question now. Do you remember any day in the course of the autumn of 1992 that you went there, that you went looking for food?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. On the 5th of October 1992, I went again together with Ibrahim following his request and we got my father to lend us a horse and we went looking for food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, could you please pause a second now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the witness the map which is Prosecution document P375? It is the blownup representation of the Fakovici area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, could you take a look at this map? Are you in a position to show the Trial Chamber where Fakovici is, and then Pantici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Pantici. Just a moment. Here's Fakovici. Pantici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what Pantici is?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, it is a part of Fakovici, the main part of Fakovici. There are houses there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 5th of October, when you said you set out together with Ibrahim, how far did you get, in fact?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I got to the upper Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: There was an ambush, and many people were killed. My father's horse was killed as well, and Ibrahim was wounded, seriously wounded, and so we had to turn back immediately because there were quite a few people who were wounded. Ibrahim was wounded as well and later on he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So basically he died in that very day?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whilst you were in the area, as far as you could get, could you see -- from that spot, could you see anything in Pantici? And you said about Pantici that it is the centre of Fakovici, basically. What were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: We could see an antiaircraft gun which was next to the school at Pantici and there were machine-guns from houses. You could see how they were mounting on to houses and there was a yellow gun with these PAM and PAT guns, anti-aircraft machine-guns and guns, and they were being used in order to shoot at people who were looking for food. And dozens of people were killed and wounded on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said to us because were you ambushed and because there were people who were wounded, you had to go back to the village. Did you talk to any of the people who managed to get to Fakovici itself?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to the refugees from Abdulici, Zanjevo, who said that there was indeed that yellow truck in Fakovici with the antiaircraft machine-guns and antiaircraft guns, that there were lots of different types of weapons, a lot of ammunition, especially at the school in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And have I understood you correctly in the sense that you yourself saw that yellow truck?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say I saw that yellow truck. That was in action.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramic, on the basis of what you yourself saw and experienced on that day, and on the basis of what you heard from the fighters, from those armed individuals or refugees or whoever, who had been into Fakovici itself, can you reply, could you just tell us, I'm trying to clarify here and I can see that Mr. Di Fazio is getting ready to react. Perhaps this reaction is justified so I'm going to try and ask a specific question. Who exactly did you talk to when you went back to your village out of this group of people who had been to Fakovici itself?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: I talked to Eniz Smajlovic [phoen] from Zanjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Can you tell me on the basis of what you heard from him and on the basis of your own experience on that day and on the basis of what you yourself saw at Fakovici, can you reply to the following question: If anyone were to claim that Fakovici did not have any sort of organised military units and simply they had village guards there, on that day, and prior to that, would that be a true statement? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If anyone were to claim that Fakovici, prior to that day, only had village guards and did not have any organised military units, would that be correct on the basis of your own experience?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: Of course not. I said earlier on that they had the weapons that I myself saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I am going to ask another question. In the course of the events, in the course of the summer 1992, did you, in Poznanovici and Podkorjen and in the area that you were spending time in, did you have any kind of communication links?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you just one more question, Mr. Ramic. Today, you described quite a few crimes to us, and you said that they were perpetrated by Serbs in May and June 1992. You mentioned that you were in an eyewitness to some of these crimes and that you have knowledge of some of these murders and about the torching of the Muslim villages, of the entire area. Now, my question to you is this: After the fall of your villages, and after the demilitarisation, did the so-called authorities in Srebrenica carry out any investigations at all with regard to those crimes perpetrated against Muslims in your area and their property?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC
utterances.text: No. There were no conditions for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just need a minute. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. I take it that you will start tomorrow. Yes. All right. And if you do require some time, you just let us know so that we will try and accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that courtesy, Your Honours, but I don't anticipate that there will be a need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You anticipate that you will be able to conclude your cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll adjourn hoping that everyone will be in fine shape tomorrow and that we will be able to continue. Mr. Ramic, we are going to stop here for today. You will be taken back to your hotel, you can rest and relax. Tomorrow you will be back with us at 9.00 tomorrow morning, and we are pretty sure that we will finish with your testimony tomorrow so that you will be able to go back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, 30 August 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
